In 2024 the United States gained two new non-invasive options for colorectal cancer screening: a cell-free DNA blood test [@chung2024shield] and a next-generation multitarget stool DNA test [@imperiale2024mtsdna]. Neither is available to the patients this project studies. Both are indicated for adults at **average risk**, and inflammatory bowel disease—chronic ulcerative colitis included—sits in the contraindication list precisely because these tests were never clinically evaluated in that population. The people at highest risk of colitis-associated colorectal cancer are the people carved out of every approved non-invasive test.

::: {.lead-panel}
## What this post is

A structured walk through the clinical questions an integrated methylation + sIgA signal would have to answer before it could change anything in a gastroenterology clinic. It is a **hypothetical care-pathway analysis**, written for clinicians. Nothing here reports performance from this cohort; the study is exploratory, cross-sectional, and has 18 participants.
:::


## What happens today to a patient with 20 years of ulcerative colitis?

They enter a colonoscopic surveillance programme. Guidelines converge on periodic examination of the whole colon with high-definition endoscopy, targeted biopsy of any visible lesion, and—depending on risk factors such as primary sclerosing cholangitis, prior neoplasia, active inflammation, or a foreshortened colon—additional random biopsies [@laine2015scenic; @murthy2021dysplasia]. The interval is set by a risk stratification that leans on inflammation history and endoscopic appearance rather than on any molecular measurement.

The programme works, but only partly. In the longest-running surveillance cohort published, 1,375 patients with ulcerative colitis were followed for 15,234 patient-years and 72 developed colorectal cancer, an incidence of 4.7 per 1,000 patient-years; rates of advanced and interval cancer fell across four decades, yet cancers kept appearing between examinations, and 37.5% of the cancers found were accompanied by synchronous cancer or spatially separate dysplasia [@choi2015surveillance]. Across 96,447 Danish and Swedish patients with ulcerative colitis, colorectal cancer incidence remained elevated against matched population controls (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.57–1.76), as did cancer-specific mortality (HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.46–1.72) [@olen2020ucrisk].

## Why isn't colonoscopy already the answer?

Because the thing being hunted is often invisible. Colitis-associated neoplasia arises in a field of chronically injured mucosa, is frequently flat rather than polypoid, and can be multifocal. The blunt summary from the ENDCaP-C investigators is that despite surveillance protocols, half of cases progress to cancer before neoplasia is detected [@beggs2019endcapc]. Chromoendoscopy improves detection—in the St Mark's cohort it was twice as effective as white-light endoscopy at finding dysplasia [@choi2015surveillance]—but adoption is uneven, it lengthens the procedure, and it does not make a diffuse molecular field change visible to the eye.

There is also the part of the problem that has nothing to do with optics. Surveillance colonoscopy requires bowel preparation, sedation, a day lost, an endoscopy slot, and a pathologist. Those are real constraints anywhere and binding constraints in a health system with limited endoscopic capacity, which is directly relevant to a Colombian cohort. Any test that could tell a clinician *which* patients most need the next slot would be doing useful work even if it never replaced a single procedure.

## Which clinical problem is actually unsolved?

The gap is specific and it is a coverage gap, not a technology gap. A blood-based cell-free DNA test detected colorectal cancer with 83% sensitivity at 90% specificity for advanced neoplasia in 7,861 average-risk adults, though sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions was only 13% [@chung2024shield]. The next-generation stool DNA test reached 93.9% sensitivity for cancer and 43.4% for advanced precancerous lesions in 20,176 participants, at 90.6% specificity for advanced neoplasia [@imperiale2024mtsdna]. These are strong screening tests. They are also, by label, for people whose colons are not chronically inflamed—and chronic inflammation is exactly the condition that changes both the biology and the base rate.

So the unsolved problem is not "detect colorectal cancer non-invasively"; that problem now has approved answers for the general population. The unsolved problem is **risk stratification inside an already-high-risk group whose mucosa is abnormal by definition**. A patient with 20 years of extensive colitis does not need to be told they are at elevated risk—they already know. They need to know whether *this year* their colon is carrying a molecular field change that warrants a closer look, and no approved test speaks to that question.

## Why a 14-gene fingerprint rather than a single marker?

Because the two things a clinician would want to separate—inflammation and neoplastic drift—are not separable by one locus. The panel deliberately spans several biological programmes: immune activation and restraint (**CD86, IL10, NLRC4, NLRP3, SIGLEC5, CLMP**), epithelial cohesion (**CDH1, CLMP**), the cell-cycle brake (**CDKN2A**), trophic signalling (**GDNF**), and neoplasia-associated markers with weaker mechanistic annotation (**FOXE1, SYNE1, FAM217B, KIAA1614, RIBC2**). The [Reactome synthesis](../reactome-gene-relations-colitis-colon-cancer/index.qmd) shows why that spread matters and where the annotation runs out; the [individual gene profiles](../silenced-and-inflammatory-genes-in-colitis.qmd) give the evidence behind each.

The precedent for multiplexing is direct. In the ENDCaP-C validation, a five-marker methylation panel detected pre-cancerous and invasive neoplasia in neoplastic mucosa with an AUC of 0.83, while a four-marker panel applied to *non-neoplastic* mucosa predicted associated bowel neoplasia with an AUC of 0.68—modest, but non-zero, from tissue that looked normal [@beggs2019endcapc]. Methylation of TUBB6 discriminated dysplastic from non-dysplastic tissue with an AUC of 0.84, including in apparently normal field mucosa downstream of a lesion [@beggs2018tubb6]. A field signal that survives in normal-looking mucosa is exactly the kind of signal that could in principle survive into plasma.

## Why validate the same fingerprint in tissue *and* plasma?

Because they answer different halves of the question. Colonic tissue anchors the signal anatomically: if a differential methylation region shows up in the biopsy, it is at least coming from the organ of interest. Plasma is the specimen a clinic could realistically draw every six months, but it is a mixture—leukocyte-derived cell-free DNA usually dominates, and a colonic epithelial signal has to be detected against that background. Neither view is sufficient alone, which is why the study collects both from the same participant; the reasoning is set out in [why pair tissue and plasma](../why-pair-tissue-and-plasma.qmd).

Pairing turns concordance into an internal validation gate rather than an assumption. If a region is differentially methylated in tissue and the same direction of change is visible in that participant's plasma, the plasma signal has an anatomical explanation. If it is visible only in tissue, the assay may lack sensitivity at realistic tumour or epithelial fractions. If it is visible only in plasma, the likeliest explanation is cell-of-origin contamination, not a discovery. Each of those three outcomes is informative, and only the paired design can tell them apart.

## What does serum sIgA add that methylation cannot?

It measures a different thing. Methylation reports on cell state and cell of origin; secretory IgA reports on the mucosal immune barrier and its interaction with the microbiota. In a clinic, the practical value of an orthogonal axis is discrimination between two situations that look similar on an inflammatory marker alone: a colon that is inflamed, and a colon that is inflamed *and* drifting. If methylation and sIgA move together in all patients, sIgA adds little; if they dissociate in a subgroup, that dissociation is the clinically interesting signal. The [assay and rationale](../../siga-methods.qmd) set out how it is measured here.

Two caveats have to travel with any sIgA claim. First, this study measures **serum** sIgA, which is accessible but is not the same measurement as secretory IgA at the intestinal surface or in stool—that distinction is stated plainly in the [methylation vs sIgA comparison](../../approach.qmd) and it does not go away when the result is convenient. Second, a serum immune marker is dynamic: infection, treatment, and systemic immune state all move it. That makes it a plausible complement to a durable epigenetic signal and a poor substitute for one.

## Where would such a test sit in a care pathway?

Three placements are worth distinguishing, because they have different evidence requirements. **Triage before colonoscopy** would use the test to prioritise scarce endoscopy slots—it needs high sensitivity and tolerates modest specificity, because the downstream action is a procedure the patient was going to need eventually. **Surveillance-interval personalisation** would use a persistently negative result to justify extending an interval, and that is the most demanding use: it requires prospective, longitudinal evidence that a negative result predicts absence of progression, not merely absence of current dysplasia. **Post-treatment or post-resection monitoring** would track the signal over time within one patient, where each person is their own baseline and the relevant question is change rather than an absolute threshold.

None of these is a replacement for colonoscopy, and the framing matters clinically. A methylation field signal, by construction, says something about the state of the mucosa as a whole; it does not localise a lesion, and a positive result still ends in an endoscope. The realistic ambition is to change *who gets scoped next and when*, not to remove the procedure from the pathway.

## What performance would it actually need to change a decision?

There is a published bar to clear. Medicare's national coverage determination for colorectal cancer screening tests ([NCD 210.3](https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/ncd.aspx?NCDId=281)) requires a blood-based biomarker screening test to show at least **74% sensitivity** for colorectal cancer and at least **90% specificity**, based on the pivotal studies in FDA labelling, and covers such a test once every three years. That bar was calibrated against average-risk screening, and a surveillance test for high-risk colitis would ultimately need its own threshold—but it is the only concrete number the field has, and it is a reasonable place to start reasoning.

Specificity is the constraint that bites, and how hard it bites depends on prevalence—which in surveillance is neither negligible nor well pinned down. Reported per-procedure dysplasia detection varies widely with population and technique: a real-world Latin American surveillance series spanning Colombia, Costa Rica, Peru, Ecuador and the Dominican Republic found dysplasia in 12.5% of 144 surveillance colonoscopies, with digital chromoendoscopy detecting roughly five times more than white light [@parraizquierdo2025latam], while population-based cohorts report considerably lower rates [@choi2015surveillance]. That spread matters more than any single figure, and it cuts in the technology's favour: a surveillance population is enriched relative to average-risk screening, so the same test yields a better positive predictive value here than it would in a screening programme.

The arithmetic is still worth seeing before a test is called "accurate". At 5% prevalence, a test with 85% sensitivity and 90% specificity returns a positive predictive value near 31%—about three colonoscopies per true finding. At the 12.5% observed in that Latin American series, the same test returns roughly 55%. @fig-results shows the whole curve rather than a single operating point, because the honest answer depends on which population is being tested.

::: {.callout-warning title="Simulation disclaimer"}
Panels (b) and (c) of @fig-results contain **no data from this study or any other**. Panel (b) is drawn from a binormal model at chosen AUC values to illustrate the shape of the trade-off. Panel (c) is exact arithmetic — Bayes' rule applied to stated sensitivity and specificity — and is true of any test with those characteristics, including tests that do not exist.
:::

def roc_from_auc(auc, n=400):
    """Binormal ROC with equal variances: the curve implied by a given AUC."""
    from scipy.stats import norm
    mu = np.sqrt(2) * norm.ppf(auc)
    fpr = np.linspace(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4, n)
    tpr = norm.cdf(norm.ppf(fpr) + mu)
    return fpr, tpr

## How does this compare with what is already on the market?

The table below is a **clinical-indication** landscape; the [cfDNA technology landscape](../../technology.qmd) covers the same companies from the platform side. Read the *indicated population* column first—it is where the gap lives.

| [Cologuard Plus](https://www.exactsciences.com/newsroom/press-releases/fda-approves-exact-sciences-cologuard-plus-test) (Exact Sciences) | Stool | Methylated DNA markers + haemoglobin | FDA-approved Oct 2024 | Average risk, ≥45 | 93.9% cancer sensitivity, 43.4% for advanced precancerous lesions [@imperiale2024mtsdna]. IBD is a listed contraindication; the test was not evaluated in inflamed mucosa. |

Proves a blood test can be approved; says nothing about UC. |
| Epi proColon (methylated SEPT9) | Plasma | Single methylation marker | Earlier-generation blood test | Average-risk screening | 48.2% sensitivity, 91.5% specificity, 11.2% for advanced adenoma [@church2014sept9]. The clearest evidence that one marker is not enough. |

Measures inflammation, not neoplastic drift — and it is a Crohn's test. |

## What would make it fail?

Four things, in rough order of likelihood. **Inflammation confounds methylation**: several panel genes were nominated because they change with disease severity, which is exactly what makes them poor at distinguishing "severely inflamed" from "neoplastically drifting". **Leukocyte cfDNA dominates plasma**: if the colonic epithelial fraction is small, a real tissue signal may simply be undetectable at achievable sequencing depth, and tissue-of-origin deconvolution becomes a prerequisite rather than a refinement. **Batch and pre-analytics masquerade as biology**: collection tube, processing delay, freeze–thaw, and library batch can all generate group differences in a cohort this size. **The cohort is too small for the question**: with 18 participants across three groups, this design can estimate effect sizes and check assay behaviour; it cannot estimate sensitivity, and any classifier trained on it will overfit.

There is also a conceptual limit that no amount of data removes. A field-change marker reports on the state of the mucosa, not the location of a lesion. Even a well-performing test would end in a colonoscopy, and its value would have to be argued in terms of *better-targeted* endoscopy rather than *less* endoscopy.

## What is the shortest credible path to a clinic?

Each rung requires a different study, and the study described on this site sits on the first. Association—do the signals differ across groups?—is answerable now. Discrimination in held-out data needs a cohort perhaps an order of magnitude larger, with pre-specified regions and honest resampling. Prognosis needs longitudinal follow-up in a surveillance programme, because the clinically relevant outcome is progression, not cross-sectional group membership. Clinical utility needs a comparison against the current pathway, and reimbursement needs performance characteristics documented in a form a payer recognises.

The honest summary is that the clinical problem is real, well-characterised, and unaddressed by any approved test, and that this project is at rung one of five. That is a reason to be precise about which rung each claim belongs to, not a reason to discount the question.

::: {.callout-important title="Translation boundary"}
This post describes clinical problems an integrated methylation and sIgA signal *could* address if it validated. It reports no performance from this cohort, provides no medical advice, and is not evidence that methylation or serum sIgA predicts an individual's cancer risk. Nothing here supports substituting any measurement for colonoscopic surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease. The named commercial tests are described by their published indications and evidence; none is endorsed, and none is indicated for ulcerative colitis surveillance.
